reading.body:
CyrusOne's Lebanon, Ohio campus publishes 12 megawatts of IT capacity across 400,000 square feet of technical space, the largest published power figure among the eight Ohio facilities that report one.

That ratio works out to roughly 30 watts per square foot, which is enterprise colocation density rather than AI training density. The certification list, SOC 2 Type 2, PCI DSS, HIPAA, ISO 27001, FISMA, SSAE 16 Type II and Green Globes, describes a facility built for regulated healthcare, finance and federal workloads. Those tenants value compliance and redundancy, not the highest possible power draw per rack.

For AI specifically, 12 megawatts is modest. The rack count of roughly 300 depends on an assumed 40 kilowatts per rack, which is a modeling choice and not a published specification. Ohio's published data center load totals 60.4 megawatts across 77 mapped facilities, but only 8 of those report power figures at all, so that total is a floor rather than a census of what the state actually draws.

What the record does not contain is the part that decides whether this site matters for AI scaling. There is no published grid connection capacity, no announced expansion, no tenant list and no pricing. The suitability score of 58 is computed from published IT capacity and operator type alone, and it flags announced expansion as missing. Whether Lebanon can host sustained high-density load depends on utility capacity and operator intent, and neither is in the data.

suitability.basis: weighted mean of the published inputs named here, scaled to 100; formula on the methodology page
